rv.q: National treasure Griff Rhys Jones is a hoot as Jim Hacker, while Clive Francis is great value opposite him. While not in the same league as the original, it is an enjoyable, nostalgic coda – oddly topical and surprisingly poignant, too. Directing the show, Lynn – who co-wrote the series with Antony Jay – has cooked up a spicy scenario.
If this swansong is slapdash and indulgent, he’s surely earned the right to it.
But Lynn’s perspective is arresting on age, irrelevance and their levelling effects – and the characters’ company is as charming as ever.
Ultimately, this is an affectionate portrait and a fond farewell to the familiar characters in their last years.
Instead, where the play works best is the elegiac tone it strikes.
I’m Sorry, Prime Minister is brilliant, deliciously sharp, and deeply poignant.
To know what he means by that, you have to catch Oliver Kaderbhai’s seamless production.
Even if it feels contrived, it is a nostalgic and enjoyable antidote to the grim farce being staged by our current government.
Overall, it’s an affable evening that many boomers who are no longer working full-time will warm to.
But ultimately, its directionless satire of woke politics doesn’t just lose the plot – it forgets it was meant to be looking for one.
This is political comedy of the highest order: elegant, incisive and poignant.
This is political satire with heart, intelligence and enormous charm, and it brings the saga of Hacker and Humphrey to a close with laughter and real poignancy.
Rhys Jones and Francis are on dazzling form as the ageing heavyweights dragged out of retirement for one last punch-up.
This one is much better: years have passed, and this is a final lap of honour for the pair as old codgers, facing what we all do in declining years and significance.
Unfortunately, the stage production I’M SORRY PRIME MINISTER (penned and directed by Lynn himself) proves something of a flabby, self-flagellating foot-note.
The sense lingers that perhaps, like the characters themselves, the show might have been content to retire quietly rather than stretch towards one final bow.
Crucially, Francis appears to be enjoying it every bit as much as we are, an underrated skill in comic acting.
Opposite him is the only actor seen in the earlier version of this play: as Sir Humphrey, Clive Francis is an absolute delight.

cn.t: A bittersweet finale to the beloved franchise finds Hacker and Humphrey in old age, delivering witty political satire that remains sharp and relevant, though Griff Rhys Jones' broad performance and uneven pacing prevent it from matching its predecessors' brilliance.
